question: a) Write the electronic configurations of Cr and Cu and explain why they are exceptions. [2] b) Why is zinc not regarded as a transition element? [1] c) Why are Sc³⁺ and Zn²⁺ colourless? [1] d) How many d electrons has Cr in [Cr(H₂O)₆]³⁺? [1]
answer: (a) Cr: [Ar] 3d⁵4s¹ (not 3d⁴4s²) and Cu: [Ar] 3d¹⁰4s¹ (not 3d⁹4s²). A half-filled (d⁵) or fully filled (d¹⁰) subshell has extra stability from symmetry and exchange energy, so one 4s electron moves into the 3d subshell.(b) Zn is [Ar] 3d¹⁰4s² and forms only Zn²⁺ (3d¹⁰): its d subshell is full in both the atom and its common ion, so it does not meet the definition of a transition element (an ion with a partly filled d subshell).(c) Sc³⁺ is 3d⁰ and Zn²⁺ is 3d¹⁰, so there is no partly filled d subshell and no d–d transition is possible.(d) Cr³⁺ is [Ar] 3d³: three d electrons.
anchor: A transition element has a partially filled d subshell in the atom or in a common ion. Zn (3d¹⁰4s², Zn²⁺ = 3d¹⁰) is therefore not typical.

question: a) Write the Hofmann bromamide reaction for ethanamide. [2] b) Why is an amide amphoteric? [1] c) Arrange acid chloride, anhydride, ester and amide in decreasing order of reactivity towards nucleophiles. [1] d) What is the Claisen condensation? [1]
answer: (a) CH₃CONH₂ + Br₂ + 4NaOH → CH₃NH₂ + Na₂CO₃ + 2NaBr + 2H₂O (a primary amine with one carbon fewer).(b) An amide can accept a proton on its nitrogen lone pair (weakly basic) and can lose an N–H proton to a strong base such as sodium, forming a salt (weakly acidic); it is amphoteric.(c) Acid chloride > anhydride > ester > amide.(d) Claisen condensation: two molecules of an ester with α-hydrogens condense in the presence of sodium ethoxide to give a β-keto ester: 2CH₃COOC₂H₅ → (C₂H₅ONa) CH₃COCH₂COOC₂H₅ + C₂H₅OH (ethyl acetoacetate).
anchor: (d) An amide can gain a proton on the N lone pair (weakly basic, forming a salt with a strong acid such as RCONH₂·HCl) and can lose an N–H proton to a strong base or to sodium (weakly acidic, RCONHNa), so it is amphoteric.

question: a) How would you separate them by Hoffmann's method? [3] b) Give the nitrous acid test to distinguish A from B. [2] (NEB 2082)
answer: (a) Heat the mixture with diethyl oxalate. Propylamine (A) forms the solid N,N′-dipropyloxamide, (CONHC₃H₇)₂, and N-methylethanamine (B) forms the liquid oxamic ester, C₂H₅OOC–CO–N(CH₃)C₂H₅. The liquid is distilled off (or the solid is filtered), and each is hydrolysed with KOH to regenerate the amine.(b) Nitrous acid test (NaNO₂ + HCl): A, a primary amine, gives colourless gas bubbles of N₂ and the alcohol: CH₃CH₂CH₂NH₂ + HNO₂ → CH₃CH₂CH₂OH + N₂↑ + H₂O. question: a) How is a Grignard reagent prepared from a haloalkane and from a haloarene? [2] b) Why must the preparation be carried out in dry ether? [1] c) Write the reaction of CH₃MgBr with water. [1] d) What product results from CH₃MgBr and HCN? [1]
answer: (a) From a haloalkane: CH₃CH₂Br + Mg → (dry ether) CH₃CH₂MgBr. From a haloarene: C₆H₅Br + Mg → (dry ether, or THF) C₆H₅MgBr.(b) Grignard reagents are strongly basic and are destroyed by any water or alcohol; ether also dissolves the reagent by co-ordinating to magnesium.(c) CH₃MgBr + H₂O → CH₄ + Mg(OH)Br.(d) With HCN the Grignard reagent takes up the acidic hydrogen: CH₃MgBr + HCN → CH₄ + Mg(CN)Br (so HCN is a proton source; addition to a nitrile carbon needs RCN, not HCN).

question: a) Define condensation polymerisation and give the monomers of Bakelite. [2] b) How are addition and condensation polymers formed? Give one example of each. [3] (NEB 2078 model, 2082, 2079 model)
answer: (a) Condensation polymerisation is the joining of many molecules of one or more monomers, each with two or more functional groups, with the loss of a small molecule such as water or HCl at every step. Bakelite is formed from phenol (C₆H₅OH) and methanal (HCHO).(b) Addition polymers are formed by the repeated addition of unsaturated monomers (alkenes) with no loss of atoms: n CH₂=CH₂ → (–CH₂–CH₂–)n, polythene. Condensation polymers are formed from bifunctional monomers with elimination of water: n H₂N(CH₂)₆NH₂ + n HOOC(CH₂)₄COOH → nylon 6,6 + 2n H₂O.
anchor: Answer: addition: no loss of atoms (polythene); condensation: loss of H₂O or HCl (nylon 6,6 from H₂N(CH₂)₆NH₂ and HOOC(CH₂)₄COOH; Bakelite from phenol and methanal; polystyrene from styrene).

unit: Nuclear Chemistry and Applications of Radioactivity
question: a) Why is nuclear fusion also called a thermonuclear reaction? [2] b) Write one fusion reaction and one fission reaction. [2] c) Why does fusion release more energy per kilogram of fuel than fission? [1] (NEB 2082 for (a))
answer: (a) Fusion needs a temperature of about 10⁷–10⁸ K to give the nuclei enough kinetic energy to overcome the electrostatic repulsion between them, so it is called a thermonuclear reaction (as in the Sun).(b) Fusion: ²₁H + ³₁H → ⁴₂He + ¹₀n + 17.6 MeV. Fission: ²³⁵₉₂U + ¹₀n → ¹⁴¹₅₆Ba + ⁹²₃₆Kr + 3¹₀n + energy (about 200 MeV per nucleus).(c) The fusion fuel is made of very light nuclei, so one kilogram contains many more nuclei than a kilogram of uranium; although fission releases more energy per nucleus, fusion releases about three to four times as much energy per unit mass.
anchor: Each fission of a uranium-235 nucleus releases three neutrons, so the number of fissions can multiply 3, 9, 27 … in successive generations. Nuclear fusion is the joining of two light nuclei into a heavier one.

answer: (a) Natural radioactivity is the spontaneous emission of α, β or γ rays by heavy unstable nuclei found in nature (U, Th, Ra); artificial radioactivity is produced by bombarding a stable nucleus with particles, giving unstable isotopes (³⁰P, ²⁴Na) that then decay.(b) 25 % = ¼ = (½)², so two half-lives have elapsed.
anchor: Radioactivity is the spontaneous disintegration of an unstable nucleus with the emission of α-particles, β-particles or γ-rays.

question: Which of the following best explains why 2-chlorobutanoic acid has a lower $pK_a$ value compared to 4-chlorobutanoic acid?

why: The chlorine atom's proximity to the carboxylic group in 2-chlorobutanoic acid enhances its electron-withdrawing effect (-I effect), increasing acidity as indicated by the lower $pK_a$ value.

question: What effect does the nitro group have on the reactivity of the aromatic ring it is attached to?

question: Explain why azobenzene is not considered a dye and describe the role of auxochromes in dyes using an example.
answer: Azobenzene is not a dye because it lacks auxochromes despite having a chromophore ($-N=N-$), making it just a chromogen. Auxochromes like dimethylamino and sulphonate groups in azo dyes enhance color intensity and attach the dye to fibers.
anchor: A compound with a chromophore but no auxochrome is merely coloured (a chromogen), not a dye: azobenzene is orange but washes straight out of cloth. The azo group –N=N– is the chromophore; the dimethylamino and sulphonate groups are auxochromes, which deepen the colour and anchor the dye to the fibre. Integrated pest management uses biological pesticides, crop rotation and resistant varieties to cut chemical use. Dyes, by contrast, colour fabrics; azo dyes contain –N=N– chromophores.

question: Explain the relationship between spontaneity and the change in Gibbs free energy ($\Delta G$) in a chemical reaction.
answer: 1. A spontaneous process does not require external intervention. 2. For spontaneity, $\Delta G$ must be negative. 3. At equilibrium, $\Delta G = 0$.
anchor: A system exchanges matter and/or energy with its surroundings. $U$, $H$, $S$, $G$, $p$, $V$, $T$ are state functions; $q$ and $w$ are not. Spontaneous means "needs no help", not "happens quickly". 4.10 Relationship between $\Delta G$ and equilibrium constant.

question: What are the units of the specific reaction rate ($k$) and how does it vary with temperature?
answer: The units of specific reaction rate ($k$) are $(\text{mol L}^{-1})^{1-n}\text{s}^{-1}$. It is independent of concentration but increases with temperature.

question: Describe the components and their approximate ratio in the mixture fed into the top of the cup-and-cone arrangement.
answer: The mixture consists of calcined ore, coke, and limestone in an approximate ratio of 8:4:1. Calcined ore is treated to remove moisture, CO$_2$, sulphur, and arsenic.

answer: The molecular weight of an addition polymer is calculated as $M(polymer) = n \times M(monomer)$, where $n$ is the degree of polymerization. Integrated pest management employs biological pesticides, crop rotation, and resistant crop varieties to reduce chemical pesticide use.

question: Given the reaction of anisole ($\text{C}_7\text{H}_8\text{O}$) with excess HI, calculate the moles of products formed if you start with 10.8 g of anisole. What is the molar mass of anisole?
answer: Molar mass of anisole = 108 g/mol. Moles of anisole = $\frac{10.8\ \text{g}}{108\ \text{g/mol}} = 0.10\ \text{mol}$. One mole of anisole yields one mole of each product, thus 0.10 mol of each product forms.

question: Describe the formation and reaction of Grignard reagents, including their sensitivity to compounds with acidic hydrogens, and calculate the molar mass of propanoic acid ($\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{COOH}$) produced when a Grignard reagent reacts with carbon dioxide.
answer: Grignard reagents form in a 1:1 ratio and react with carbon dioxide to add one carbon, yielding propanoic acid ($\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{COOH}$). They must remain dry as they are destroyed by compounds with acidic hydrogens. For instance, with water: $\text{CH}_3\text{MgBr} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \Rightarrow \text{CH}_4 + \text{Mg(OH)Br}$. Propanoic acid's molar mass is calculated as $3(12) + 6(1) + 2(16) = 74 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$. This highlights the reagent's sensitivity and application in organic synthesis.

All apparatus and reagents must be perfectly dry, because Grignard reagents are destroyed by any compound with an acidic hydrogen. With water (or alcohol or amine) gives an alkane: $\text{CH}_{3}\text{MgBr} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O} \Rightarrow \text{CH}_{4} + \text{Mg(OH)Br}$. (b) The cell finds the molar mass 186.03 g/mol and the composition: 64.6 per cent carbon, 5.4 per cent hydrogen and 30.0 per cent iron. question: Compare the acidity of benzoic acid and ethanoic acid using their $pK_a$ values and explain why benzoic acid is more acidic. Also, explain the mechanism of nucleophilic addition to carboxylic acid derivatives.
answer: Benzoic acid ($pK_a$ 4.20) is more acidic than ethanoic acid ($pK_a$ 4.76) due to the electron-withdrawing effect of the sp² hybridized ring carbon in benzoic acid, which stabilizes the negative charge on the conjugate base better. In the nucleophilic addition mechanism, a nucleophile attacks the carbonyl carbon forming a tetrahedral intermediate. The leaving group departs, reforming the C=O bond. This mechanism applies to carboxylic acid derivatives like esters or amides.
anchor: For aromatic acids, benzoic acid ($pK_a$ 4.20) is stronger than ethanoic acid because the sp² ring carbon is more electronegative than an sp³ alkyl carbon. The nucleophile adds to give a tetrahedral intermediate; the leaving group L⁻ is then expelled as the C=O bond re-forms. The same argument, applied three times, gives the order that NEB asks for every year: Ethanoic acid ($pK_a$ 4.76) beats phenol ($pK_a$ 10.0) because in phenoxide the charge is spread over carbon atoms, which are less electronegative than oxygen, and only two of the contributing structures carry it.

question: Describe the mechanism of the substitution reaction of haloalkanes with a nucleophile, including the rate law and the orientation of attack by different reagents such as potassium and silver.
answer: The substitution reaction of haloalkanes with a nucleophile follows a second-order rate law: $\text{rate} = k[\text{R–X}][\text{Nu}^{-}]$. The slow step involves breaking the C–Br bond to form a planar carbocation and Br⁻. Nucleophiles attack from the back side, causing the other three groups to push through the plane like an umbrella turning inside out. Potassium attacks through C or O, while silver attacks through N. In aqueous KOH, substitution occurs forming an alcohol; in alcoholic KOH, elimination forms an alkene, favoring the more substituted alkene per Saytzeff's rule.
anchor: $$\text{rate} = k[\text{R–X}][\text{Nu}^{-}] \quad\text{(second order)}$$ Slow step: the C–Br bond breaks to give a planar carbocation (CH₃)₃C⁺ and Br⁻. Potassium attacks through C or O, silver through N. Aqueous KOH substitutes (alcohol); alcoholic KOH eliminates (alkene), the more substituted alkene being the major product by Saytzeff's rule. $$\text{rate} = k\,[\text{R--X}]\,[\text{Nu}^-]$$ Because the nucleophile comes in from the back, the other three groups are pushed through the plane like an umbrella turning inside out in the wind.

question: Explain how the treatment of saturated brine with HCl gas leads to the precipitation of pure NaCl, considering the ion product and solubility product.
answer: HCl gas added to saturated brine increases $[\text{Cl}^{-}]$, raising $Q = [\text{Na}^{+}][\text{Cl}^{-}]$ above $K_{sp}$ for NaCl ($1.1 \times 10^{-10}$), causing NaCl precipitation. Impurities like MgCl₂ and CaCl₂ remain dissolved due to higher solubility. Precipitation stops when $Q$ equals $K_{sp}$.

question: Describe the reaction pathway of C₃H₇Br (A) leading to C₃H₆ (B) and further to C, an isomer of A, including the reagents involved and the rules governing the formation of products.
answer: A (C₃H₇Br) reacts with alcoholic KOH to form B (C₃H₆) via elimination. B then reacts with HBr, adding according to Markovnikov's rule, forming C, an isomer of A. Alcoholic KOH favors elimination, producing the more substituted alkene by Saytzeff's rule.

question: Describe the complete reduction process of an aldol condensation product using the example of $\ce{CH3CH(OH)CH2CHO}$ and state the final product formed.
answer: 1. Heating $\ce{CH3CH(OH)CH2CHO}$ causes dehydration: $\ce{CH3CH(OH)CH2CHO ->[\Delta] CH3CH=CHCHO + H2O}$. 2. Further reduction removes all oxygen, converting >C=O to >CH₂. 3. The final product is $\ce{CH3CH=CHCH3}$.

question: Given the dissociation of Ca(OH)₂ into Ca²⁺ and OH⁻ ions, calculate the [OH⁻] concentration if the initial concentration of Ca(OH)₂ is 0.005 mol L⁻¹. Also, explain how the degree of ionisation changes with dilution for weak acids compared to strong acids.
answer: For Ca(OH)₂, $[\text{OH}^{-}] = 2 \times 0.005 = 0.01\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$. Weak acids' ionisation increases sharply with dilution, nearing 100% at extreme dilution. Strong acids ($K_a$ larger) show higher ionisation at all concentrations.

question: Given the formula for $K_b$ of amines as $K_b = \frac{[\mathrm{RNH_3^+}][\mathrm{OH^-}]}{[\mathrm{RNH_2}]}$, explain how $K_b$ and $pK_b$ relate to the strength of the amine base.
answer: 1. Larger $K_b$ indicates stronger base due to higher concentration of $\mathrm{RNH_3^+}$ and $\mathrm{OH^-}$. 2. Smaller $pK_b$ signifies stronger base since $pK_b = -\log K_b$. 3. Stronger bases have higher $K_b$ and lower $pK_b$ values.

question: Explain how the basicity of amines is related to their $K_b$ and $pK_b$ values, and describe the boiling point trend among primary, secondary, and tertiary amines.
answer: A larger $K_b$ and smaller $pK_b$ indicate stronger bases. Boiling points follow: primary > secondary > tertiary due to hydrogen bonding; amines have lower boiling points than similar mass alcohols.

question: Calculate the pH of a buffer solution containing 0.2 M CH₃COOH and 0.1 M CH₃COONa, given that the pKa of CH₃COOH is 4.74. Use the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation.

question: Explain how mass and energy conservation apply to nuclear reactions using Einstein's equation.
answer: In nuclear reactions, mass $\Delta m$ is converted to energy $E = \Delta m\,c^2$. One atomic mass unit (u) converts to 931.5 MeV of energy, demonstrating mass-energy equivalence.

question: Describe the process of how wood is converted into bleached chemical pulp, including the role of alkali and HS⁻, and state the approximate yield of pulp from oven-dry wood.
answer: Alkali and HS⁻ dissolve lignin as sodium salts, leaving cellulose fibers. The spent liquor, black liquor, is burnt to recover chemicals. About 2.2 tonnes of oven-dry wood yield one tonne of bleached pulp, as half of the wood substance is dissolved.

question: Explain the rate law for the reaction of haloalkanes and what happens if the carbon attached to the halogen is chiral.
answer: The rate law for the reaction of haloalkanes is $\text{rate} = k[\text{R-X}]$, indicating first-order kinetics. If the carbon attached to the halogen is chiral, nucleophilic attack can occur from both faces, leading to a racemic mixture due to racemization.

question: Describe the reaction conditions necessary for the synthesis of Grignard reagents and their reaction with acetone to form 2-methylpropan-2-ol. Include the stoichiometric calculation for the formation of methane from an active hydrogen compound.
answer: Grignard reagents require perfectly dry apparatus and reagents; they react destructively with compounds containing acidic hydrogen like water, alcohol, or amines, yielding methane: $\text{CH}_3\text{MgBr} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \Rightarrow \text{CH}_4 + \text{Mg(OH)Br}$. Each active hydrogen yields one methane molecule; thus, moles of $\text{CH}_4$ = 0.224 / 22.4 = 0.0100 mol. Acetone reacts with $\text{CH}_3\text{MgBr}$ to produce 2-methylpropan-2-ol, a tertiary alcohol.

Each active hydrogen releases one molecule of methane: Moles of CH₄ = 0.224 / 22.4 = 0.0100 mol. With a ketone gives a tertiary alcohol: acetone + CH$_3$MgBr gives 2-methylpropan-2-ol.

question: Compare the acidity of benzoic acid ($pK_a$ 4.20) and ethanoic acid, and explain how the presence of an electron-withdrawing substituent like chlorine affects the $pK_a$ values of butanoic acid derivatives such as 2-chlorobutanoic acid and 4-chlorobutanoic acid.
answer: Benzoic acid is stronger than ethanoic acid due to the sp² ring carbon's higher electronegativity stabilizing the carboxylate ion. question: Describe the process of dissolving lignin during paper production and the chemical reaction used to produce NaOH. Include the molar calculation for NaOH production.
answer: Alkali and HS⁻ dissolve lignin into sodium salts, isolating cellulose fibers; black liquor is then burnt to recover chemicals. Reaction: $Na_2CO_3 + Ca(OH)_2 \rightarrow 2NaOH + CaCO_3\downarrow$. For NaOH, M(NaOH) = 40 g/mol, thus 1000g gives 25 kmol of NaOH.

question: Calculate the percentage of copper in CuFeS₂ and the fraction of copper in the ore if the ore contains 20.0% of CuFeS₂.
answer: The molar mass of CuFeS₂ is $183.5\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$. The percentage of Cu in CuFeS₂ is 34.60%. Thus, the fraction of copper in the ore is 6.92%.

question: Explain the crystal field splitting in transition metal complexes and the energy difference involved in electron promotion from $t_{2g}$ to $e_g$ orbitals.
answer: In transition metals, $e_g$ orbitals rise by 0.6 Δo and $t_{2g}$ fall by 0.4 Δo due to ligand interaction. Light of energy Δo promotes electrons from $t_{2g}$ to $e_g$. Δo is the crystal field splitting energy.
anchor: The two $e_g$ orbitals, which point at the ligands, rise by 0.6 Δo above the average energy; the three $t_{2g}$ orbitals, which point between the ligands, fall by 0.4 Δo. Δo is the crystal field splitting energy; light of energy Δo promotes an electron from $t_{2g}$ to $e_g$.

question: Describe the reaction of diethyl ether with excess hot HI and the conditions under which ethers should be stored to prevent peroxide formation.
answer: Diethyl ether reacts with excess hot HI to form iodoethane and water: $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OC}_2\text{H}_5 + 2\text{HI} \Rightarrow 2\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{I} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$. Ethers should be stored with iron or ferrous sulfate to destroy any formed peroxides, and tested with acidified KI to detect iodine's yellow-brown color.

Ether should be tested with acidified KI (a yellow-brown colour of iodine), and stored over iron or with ferrous sulphate to destroy peroxides. The –OCH$_3$ group activates the ring and directs to the o- and p-positions, giving o- and p-bromoanisole, nitroanisole and p-methylanisole.

question: Explain the electronic configuration of transition metals in a tetrahedral field and provide the maximum oxidation states for Mn, Cr, and V based on their electron configurations.
answer: In a tetrahedral field, $e$ pair ($d_{z^2}$, $d_{x^2-y^2}$) is lower and $t_2$ trio higher. Max oxidation states: Mn (+7 in MnO₄⁻), Cr (+6 in Cr₂O₇²⁻), V (+5 in VO₃⁻).
anchor: In a tetrahedral field only four ligands approach, and they come between the axes, so the pattern is inverted: the $e$ pair ($d_{z^2}$, $d_{x^2-y^2}$) lies lower and the $t_2$ trio higher. The maximum state equals the total of 3d and 4s electrons up to manganese (Mn: 5 + 2 = +7 in MnO₄⁻; Cr: +6 in Cr₂O₇²⁻; V: +5 in VO₃⁻).

question: Derive the relationship between the rate constants $k_1$ and $k_2$ at temperatures $T_1$ and $T_2$, respectively, using the Arrhenius equation.
answer: Using the Arrhenius equation, $\log\dfrac{k_2}{k_1} = \dfrac{E_a}{2.303R}\left(\dfrac{1}{T_1} - \dfrac{1}{T_2}\right)$. This shows how rate constants change with temperature, where $E_a$ is activation energy and $R$ is the gas constant.

question: Explain why an increase in temperature significantly affects reaction rates based on the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution. Also, calculate the average rate of disappearance of N₂O₅ given its concentration changes from 0.50 to 0.40 mol L⁻¹ over 100 seconds.

For N₂O₅, the average rate of disappearance is $-\dfrac{\Delta[\text{N}_2\text{O}_5]}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{0.50 - 0.40}{100} = 1.0\times10^{-3}$ mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹.

question: Explain how the addition of 0.010 mol of HCl to one liter of pure water affects the pH and discuss the utility of a buffer within its effective pH range. Additionally, describe why Mg(OH)₂ remains in solution during the precipitation of Group III A elements as hydroxides using NH₄OH and NH₄Cl.
answer: 1. Adding 0.010 mol HCl to 1 L water changes pH from 7 to $-\log(0.010) = 2$, a decrease of 5 pH units. 2. Buffers are effective over $pH = pK_a \pm 1$. 3. NH₄⁺ ions from NH₄Cl suppress NH₄OH ionization, maintaining low $[\text{OH}^-]$. 4. Only hydroxides with very low $K_{sp}$ precipitate due to limited $[\text{OH}^-]$. 5. Mg(OH)₂, having higher $K_{sp}$, remains dissolved under these conditions.
anchor: Group III A (Fe³⁺, Al³⁺, Cr³⁺) is precipitated as hydroxides by NH₄OH in the presence of NH₄Cl. The NH₄⁺ common ion suppresses the ionisation of NH₄OH, keeping $[\text{OH}^{-}]$ low, so only the hydroxides of very low $K_{sp}$ come down and Mg(OH)₂ stays in solution. In practice a buffer is useful only over the range $pH = pK_a \pm 1$. The same 0.010 mol of HCl added to a litre of pure water would take the pH from 7 to $-\log(0.010) = 2$ — a change of five units. 2.13 Indicators and selection of indicators in acid-base titration.

question: Explain the principle behind the conversion of mass into energy in nuclear reactions using Einstein's equation and calculate the energy released when 1 atomic mass unit (u) is converted into energy.
answer: The principle of mass-energy conversion in nuclear reactions is governed by Einstein's equation $E = \Delta m\,c^2$. Here, a small mass loss ($\Delta m$) is transformed into a large amount of energy. Each atomic mass unit (1 u) corresponds to 931.5 MeV of energy upon complete conversion. For instance, if 1 u is lost, the energy released is calculated as follows: $E = 1 \text{ u} \times 931.5 \text{ MeV} = 931.5 \text{ MeV}$. This concept applies to both nuclear fission and fusion reactions where mass is lost and converted into energy.
anchor: The source is the mass defect, converted by Einstein's relation $E = \Delta m\,c^{2}$, where 1 atomic mass unit corresponds to 931.5 MeV. The SI unit of activity is the becquerel (1 decay per second); 1 curie = $3.7 \times 10^{10}$ Bq. Mass and energy together are conserved: the small mass loss Δm appears as energy, $E = \\Delta m\\,c^2$, where 1 u releases 931.5 MeV. 21.4 Nuclear fission and fusion reactions.

question: (a) Derive the integrated rate equation for a first-order reaction showing that $k = \frac{2.303}{t} \log\left[\frac{a}{(a - x)}\right]$, and prove that the half-life ($t_{1/2}$) is independent of the initial concentration. [3]
answer: 1. Start with $\frac{dx}{dt} = k(a-x)$; integrate to get $\int_{0}^{x} \frac{dx}{a-x} = \int_{0}^{t} k dt$. 2. This yields $-\ln(a-x)+\ln a = kt$ or $\ln\left(\frac{a}{a-x}\right)=kt$. 3. Rearrange as $k = \frac{2.303}{t} \log\left(\frac{a}{a-x}\right)$; for $t_{1/2}$, $x=a/2$, thus $t_{1/2}=\frac{0.693}{k}$, independent of $a$.

question: Calculate the hydraulic modulus and silica modulus of cement based on the given values. Discuss the significance of these moduli in determining the lime content in cement. Also, explain how the presence of inert fly ash affects the heat of hydration of cement.
answer: The hydraulic modulus is $\frac{64}{21+6+3}=2.13$, and the silica modulus is $\frac{21}{6+3}=2.33$. A hydraulic modulus close to 2 indicates acceptable lime content, slightly high here, requiring monitoring of free lime. Silica modulus over 2 ensures proper setting properties. Inert fly ash reduces the heat of hydration; with 30% replacement, the heat falls to 305 kJ/kg, a 30% reduction from pure cement.
anchor: $$\text{hydraulic modulus} = \frac{64}{21+6+3} = \frac{64}{30} = 2.13$$ $$\text{silica modulus} = \frac{21}{6+3} = \frac{21}{9} = 2.33$$ The hydraulic modulus is close to the required value of about 2, so the lime content is acceptable — a little high, so free lime must be watched. It is a mixture of calcium silicates and aluminates made by heating limestone and clay. Limestone (CaCO$_3$), about 75–80%, is the source of lime. With 30 % replacement by inert fly ash, only 0.70 kg of cement is present, so q = 0.70 × 435 = 305 kJ per kg of blended cement, a fall of 30 %.

question: Explain why Grignard reagents require perfectly dry conditions and describe what happens when they react with water and ethylene oxide.
answer: Grignard reagents need dry conditions as they react with compounds having acidic hydrogens. With water, $\text{CH}_{3}\text{MgBr} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O} \Rightarrow \text{CH}_{4} + \text{Mg(OH)Br}$. Reacting with ethylene oxide produces a primary alcohol with two additional carbons: $\text{RMgX} \Rightarrow \text{RCH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$.
anchor: All apparatus and reagents must be perfectly dry, because Grignard reagents are destroyed by any compound with an acidic hydrogen. With water (or alcohol or amine) gives an alkane: $\text{CH}_{3}\text{MgBr} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O} \Rightarrow \text{CH}_{4} + \text{Mg(OH)Br}$. With ethylene oxide gives a primary alcohol with two extra carbon atoms: $\text{RMgX} \Rightarrow \text{RCH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$.

question: Describe the chemical process involved in the formation of clinker in cement production and state its environmental impact.
answer: At 900 °C, limestone decomposes into CaO and CO2 ($\text{CaCO}_3 \to \text{CaO} + \text{CO}_2$). Lime then reacts with silica, alumina, and iron oxide to form clinker nodules. This process contributes to 7-8% of global CO2 emissions.

question: What is the formula for calculating the instantaneous rate of reaction with respect to reactant R?
anchor: The instantaneous rate is the rate at one particular moment — the limit of the average rate as the interval shrinks to zero: $$r_{\text{inst}} = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0} \left(-\frac{\Delta[\text{R}]}{\Delta t}\right) = -\frac{d[\text{R}]}{dt}$$

question: Which of the following properties is NOT a state function?

question: Which of the following best describes the role of $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ in the reaction between iodide ($\text{I}^-$) and persulfate ($\text{S}_2\text{O}_8^{2-}$)?

question: Why does the decomposition become spontaneous above a certain temperature?

why: The oxidation reaction at the anode in a Daniell cell is represented by $\text{Zn} \to \text{Zn}^{2+} + 2e^-$.

question: Which reagent and condition is appropriate to fully hydrogenate but-2-enal to butan-1-ol?

question: What happens when solid NaCl is added to a soap solution after saponification?
answer: The concentration of $\text{Na}^{+}$ ions increases, exceeding the solubility product of sodium stearate and causing the soap to separate as a curd.

question: In the process of smelting copper, what role does silica play?

anchor: The roasted mass, mixed with coke and silica (sand), is smelted in a small water-jacketed blast furnace. Silica is the flux; it removes iron as a fusible slag: FeO + SiO₂ → FeSiO₃ (fusible slag, tapped off) The molten product that collects below the slag is copper matte, a mixture of Cu₂S and FeS containing about 45% copper. 4.

question: Why does $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ act as a catalyst in the reaction between iodide ($\text{I}^-$) and persulfate ($\text{S}_2\text{O}_8^{2-}$)?
answer: It transfers electrons to iodide and receives them back from persulfate, creating a lower-energy reaction pathway.
anchor: The metal can hand electrons to one reactant and take them from another, forming an unstable intermediate that provides a lower-energy path. Fe³⁺ catalysing the reaction of iodide with persulphate is the classic example: Fe³⁺ oxidises I⁻ and is then re-oxidised by S₂O₈²⁻.

answer: The sum of the mass numbers and atomic numbers must be equal on both sides of the equation.
anchor: Use proper nuclear notation with the mass number above and the atomic number below, and check that both add up on the two sides of every equation — a balanced nuclear equation is where the marks are.
distractors: The atomic numbers must be the same on both sides of the equation.
The mass numbers must be the same on both sides of the equation.
The elements involved must have the same chemical properties.
why: A balanced nuclear equation requires that both the mass numbers and atomic numbers are conserved across the reaction.

question: Which of the following statements correctly describes the oxidation states of iron produced by different reagents?
anchor: Pure iron is a lustrous, silvery-white, soft metal of density 7.86 g cm⁻³ and melting point 1535 °C. Note that dilute acids give iron(II), while chlorine and hot concentrated sulphuric acid give iron(III): the halogen and the hot acid are the stronger oxidising agents.
distractors: Hot concentrated sulfuric acid produces $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ ions.
Iron does not react with dilute acids.

question: What best describes the nature of a drug as defined in chemistry?
answer: A chemical substance, natural or synthetic, of low molecular mass that interacts with a biological target to provide a therapeutic effect.

Any substance that provides immediate relief without interacting with biological targets.
A natural compound only, used for the prevention of diseases.

question: Which of the following best describes a primary amine?

question: Why is mercury stored and transported in iron bottles?
answer: Iron does not form an amalgam with mercury.

distractors: Iron bottles are cheaper than other materials.
Mercury evaporates quickly when in contact with iron.
why: Iron and platinum do not amalgamate with mercury, making iron bottles suitable for storage and transportation.

question: Why can oxalic acid be used as a primary standard in volumetric analysis?
answer: It is pure, stable, and has a high equivalent weight, allowing it to be weighed directly.
anchor: A primary standard (oxalic acid, Na₂CO₃, K₂Cr₂O₇) is pure, stable and of high equivalent weight, so it can be weighed directly; a secondary standard (HCl, NaOH, KMnO₄, Na₂S₂O₃) must be titrated against one.
distractors: It can be easily synthesized in the laboratory.
It reacts faster than other acids in titration processes.
It is less expensive compared to other standard substances.

question: What type of organic compounds contains a carbonyl carbon bonded to at least one hydrogen atom?
anchor: In an aldehyde the carbonyl carbon carries at least one hydrogen; in a ketone it carries two carbon groups. That single difference in substitution controls everything in this unit — which reagent oxidises which, which compound gives a silver mirror, and which one condenses with itself.

question: Why does potassium permanganate (KMnO₄) serve as its own indicator in titration reactions?
answer: The purple MnO₄⁻ is decolourised as long as reductant remains, and the first permanent pale-pink tinge marks the endpoint.

Its color changes from green to blue as it reacts with the reducing agent.
KMnO₄ changes color based on the pH level of the solution.
why: The purple MnO₄⁻ is decolourised as long as reductant remains, and the first permanent pale-pink tinge is the end point.

question: Which of the following items commonly found in the Kathmandu Valley is traditionally made from copper or its alloys?

question: What is established between a metal and its solution when they are in contact and at equilibrium in electrochemical processes?
answer: The potential difference that develops between the metal and its solution.
anchor: This electrical double layer stops the process almost at once, and an equilibrium potential difference is set up across the metal–solution boundary. The concentration gradient of ions between the metal and the solution.
The current flow between the metal and the solution.

question: What term describes a ring formed by a poly-dentate ligand?

question: Which of the following statements correctly describes the reaction of ammoniacal silver nitrate with aldehydes and ketones?
answer: Aldehydes reduce ammoniacal silver nitrate, depositing metallic silver as a mirror on the glass.

Both aldehydes and ketones reduce ammoniacal silver nitrate, forming a mirror-like deposit.
Neither aldehydes nor ketones react with ammoniacal silver nitrate.

question: Which of the following statements correctly describes the acid hydrolysis of an ester, $\text{CH}_3\text{COOC}_2\text{H}_5 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{COOH} + \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}$?

Iodine forms the strongest bond with carbon, ensuring its quick departure.

question: What term describes a species that can donate a lone pair of electrons?
anchor: A Lewis acid is any species that can accept a lone pair of electrons; a Lewis base is any species that can donate a lone pair. Neutralisation is the formation of a coordinate (dative) bond between them.

question: In chemical kinetics, what does the valency factor specifically refer to in a reaction?

question: What characteristic feature defines an organometallic compound?
anchor: An organometallic compound contains a direct metal–carbon bond. That single requirement is what makes these compounds so useful: in almost every other organic molecule carbon is the electron-poor end of its bonds, but a metal is less electronegative than carbon, so here the carbon is electron-rich and behaves as a carbanion.
distractors: A double bond between two carbon atoms
A carbon atom bonded to hydrogen only
why: An organometallic compound contains a direct metal--carbon bond.

question: Which statement best describes a feature of a hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell used in space missions like the Apollo spacecraft?

question: Describe the process of zinc acting as a sacrificial anode over iron and the chemical behavior of copper in different environments, including its reaction with aqueous ammonia.

Copper remains unaffected by dilute HCl or H₂SO₄ but dissolves in HNO₃ and hot concentrated H₂SO₄. In the presence of aqueous ammonia, copper forms a deep blue complex ion, Cu(NH₃)₄²⁺, known as Schweitzer's reagent. This demonstrates copper's ability to form coordination complexes under specific conditions.
anchor: Because zinc has the lower electrode potential (-0.76 V against -0.44 V for iron) it is oxidised first even where the coating is scratched. Copper is unattacked by dilute HCl or H₂SO₄ but dissolves in HNO₃ and in hot conc. H₂SO₄; with aqueous ammonia and air it gives deep blue Cu(NH₃)₄₂, Schweitzer's reagent. The method is the carbon reduction of the oxide in a blast furnace, a steel tower about 30 m high lined with fire brick.

question: Explain why the statement 'the heat of the system is 200 J' is incorrect and provide the correct way to express this. Additionally, state the principle regarding the conservation of energy.
answer: The statement is incorrect because heat is not a property of the system but an energy transfer. Correctly: 'The system absorbed 200 J of heat.' The principle of conservation of energy states that energy cannot be created or destroyed, only converted from one form to another.
anchor: The imaginary boundary between them decides what can cross it. Saying "the heat of the system is 200 J" is wrong; "the system absorbed 200 J of heat" is right. Energy can neither be created nor destroyed, although it may be converted from one form to another.

question: Describe the manufacturing process of cement and differentiate between OPC and PPC grades.
answer: Cement is made from limestone, clay, and additives, processed through crushing, burning in a rotary kiln, and final grinding with gypsum. OPC grades (33, 43, 53) indicate compressive strength in MPa after 28 days. PPC contains 15–35% fly ash or pozzolana, offering better sulfate resistance and reduced heat.
anchor: Raw materials: calcareous (limestone), argillaceous (clay), correctives (sand, bauxite, iron ore) and 2–5 % gypsum added after burning. Three stages: crushing/grinding (wet or dry process) → burning in a rotary kiln → final grinding with gypsum. OPC (ordinary Portland cement) is graded 33, 43 or 53, according to the compressive strength in MPa after 28 days; PPC (Portland pozzolana cement) has 15–35% fly ash or pozzolana and is more resistant to sulphates and gives less heat.

question: In an ideal case, 10 g of salt cools 100 g of water by 7.4 K and 40 g of salt cools it by 26.3 K. Calculate the change in temperature when 20 g of salt is added to 100 g of water.
answer: 1. Use proportional relationship: $\frac{10 \text{ g}}{7.4 \text{ K}} = \frac{20 \text{ g}}{x \text{ K}}$. 2. Solve for x: $x = 2 \times 7.4 \text{ K} = 14.8 \text{ K}$. 3. Change in temperature with 20 g of salt is 14.8 K.
anchor: The imaginary boundary between them decides what can cross it. The cell divides the heat absorbed by the heat capacity of 100 g of water and the salt: 10 g of salt cools the water by 7.4 K and 40 g by 26.3 K in the ideal case.

question: Describe the properties and synthesis of ethers including any industrial applications.
answer: Ethers are synthesized via Williamson synthesis, suitable for simple ethers but yields multiple products with alcohol mixtures. They are generally inert but cleaved by HI in the Zeisel method to detect methoxy groups. Diethyl ether is highly volatile, flammable, and heavier than air, requiring storage away from flames; lower ethers are colorless, volatile, sweet-smelling liquids or gases.
anchor: Diethyl ether is highly volatile and flammable, and its vapour is heavier than air, so it must be kept away from flames. Ethers are made by Williamson synthesis, are chemically fairly inert, and are cleaved by HI, which also forms the basis of the Zeisel method for finding methoxy groups. This is cheap and is used industrially, but it works only for simple ethers — a mixture of two alcohols would give all three possible products. Methoxymethane and methoxyethane are gases at room temperature; the rest of the lower ethers are colourless, volatile, very inflammable liquids with a sweet smell.

unit: Nuclear Chemistry and Applications of Radioactivity
question: Explain the main dangers associated with nuclear reactors and provide examples of incidents where these dangers were realized.
answer: The main dangers include steam or hydrogen explosions and release of radioactive fission products. These occurred at Chernobyl (1986) due to a steam explosion and subsequent fire, and at Fukushima (2011) due to hydrogen explosions following a tsunami-induced loss of coolant.
anchor: Radiation causes somatic and genetic damage; limits are 1 mSv yr⁻¹ (public) and 20 mSv yr⁻¹ (workers); protect by distance, shielding and time. Distinguish between natural and artificial radioactivity with one example of each. The real dangers of a reactor are a steam or hydrogen explosion and the escape of radioactive fission products — what happened at Chernobyl (1986) and Fukushima (2011).

question: Explain the effect of substituents on the basicity of amines and describe what happens when amines react with diethyl oxalate and how they can be recovered.
answer: Substituents affect amine basicity: electron-releasing groups increase, electron-withdrawing decrease it. Diethyl oxalate reacts to form a solid oxamide with primary, a liquid oxamic ester with secondary, and leaves tertiary unchanged. KOH hydrolysis recovers original amines.
anchor: Substituents on the ring shift the value predictably — electron-releasing groups raise basicity, electron-withdrawing groups lower it: Overall: aliphatic amine > ammonia > aniline > diphenylamine > triphenylamine. 16.9 Alkylation, acylation, diazotisation, carbylamine and coupling. Answer: diethyl oxalate makes the primary amine a solid oxamide, the secondary a liquid oxamic ester and leaves the tertiary unchanged; KOH hydrolysis recovers them.

question: Explain why a solution of NaCl is neutral despite Cl⁻ being the conjugate base of HCl, and define Lewis acids and bases using the concept of lone pair electrons.
answer: Cl⁻, though a conjugate base of HCl, does not hydrolyze in water to change pH, keeping NaCl solution neutral. A Lewis acid accepts a lone pair ($\text{e}^-$), while a Lewis base donates it, forming a coordinate bond.
anchor: Cl⁻ is the conjugate base of HCl, but a solution of NaCl is neutral. A Lewis acid is any species that can accept a lone pair of electrons; a Lewis base is any species that can donate a lone pair. Neutralisation is the formation of a coordinate (dative) bond between them.

question: What distinguishes a primary standard like oxalic acid from a secondary standard such as HCl in volumetric analysis?
answer: A primary standard (e.g., oxalic acid) is pure, stable, and has a high equivalent weight, allowing direct weighing. A secondary standard (e.g., HCl) lacks these properties and needs titration against a primary standard.
anchor: A primary standard (oxalic acid, Na₂CO₃, K₂Cr₂O₇) is pure, stable and of high equivalent weight, so it can be weighed directly; a secondary standard (HCl, NaOH, KMnO₄, Na₂S₂O₃) must be titrated against one.

question: Explain how KMnO₄ acts as a self-indicating reagent in titration and write the balanced chemical equation for its reaction with FeSO₄.
answer: KMnO₄ acts as a self-indicator due to its purple color; it decolorizes until excess appears as a pale-pink tinge, marking the endpoint. Balanced equation: $2KMnO_4 + 10FeSO_4 + 8H_2SO_4 \rightarrow K_2SO_4 + 2MnSO_4 + 5Fe_2(SO_4)_3 + 8H_2O$.
anchor: Volumetric work needs a common currency in which "exactly enough" can be expressed. The equivalent weight (E) of a substance is the number of parts by mass of it that combine with or displace 1.008 parts by mass of hydrogen, 8 parts of oxygen, or 35.5 parts of chlorine. KMnO₄ is self-indicating: the purple MnO₄⁻ is decolourised as long as reductant remains, and the first permanent pale-pink tinge is the end point. 2KMnO₄ + 5H₂C₂O₄ + 3H₂SO₄ → K₂SO₄ + 2MnSO₄ + 10CO₂ + 8H₂O 2KMnO₄ + 10FeSO₄ + 8H₂SO₄ → K₂SO₄ + 2MnSO₄ + 5Fe₂(SO₄)₃ + 8H₂O Dichrometry.

question: Explain the role of copper and zinc in an electrochemical cell using the given reduction potentials, and identify which is the anode and which is the cathode.
answer: Copper has a more positive reduction potential than zinc, making it the cathode where reduction occurs. Zinc has a lower reduction potential, acting as the anode where oxidation takes place. Thus, $Cu^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow Cu$ at cathode and $Zn \rightarrow Zn^{2+} + 2e^-$ at anode.
anchor: Li K Ca Na Mg Al Zn Fe Ni Sn Pb H Cu Hg Ag Pt Au — "Little Katie Can Name Mg All Zinc Ferrous Nickel Snow Pblue Here Cup Hg Again Pt, Au." Everything above hydrogen displaces it from dilute acids; everything below does not. Copper has the higher (more positive) reduction potential, so copper is reduced and is the cathode; zinc is oxidised at the anode.

question: Explain why the chord is steeper than the tangent in a concentration-time curve and state the SI unit for the rate of reaction.
answer: The chord is steeper than the tangent as it represents the average rate between two points, indicating a faster initial reaction rate. The tangent shows the instantaneous rate at one point. The SI unit for the rate of reaction is $\text{mol L}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}$; for gases, $\text{atm s}^{-1}$ is also used.
anchor: The chord is steeper than the tangent because the reaction was faster earlier. Rate of reaction versus rate of change of a single species. The SI unit is mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹ (for gases, atm s⁻¹ is also used). The average rate is the slope of the chord joining two points on the concentration-time curve.

question: What are the optimal pH conditions and the mechanism involved in the reaction of aldehydes and ketones with weakly basic nitrogens?
answer: Optimal pH is 4–5; mechanism involves nucleophilic addition of nitrogen followed by dehydration of the carbinolamine.
anchor: All these reactions are fastest at about pH 4–5: enough acid to activate the carbonyl, not so much that the weakly basic nitrogen is all protonated. and the mechanism is nucleophilic addition of the nitrogen followed by dehydration of the resulting carbinolamine.

unit: Chemistry in the service of mankind
question: Write the monomer and polymerization reaction for Nylon 6,6 and state the type of polymerization involved and the small molecule lost.
answer: Monomer: Adipic acid ($\text{HOOC}(\text{CH}_2)_4\text{COOH}$) and hexamethylenediamine ($\text{H}_2\text{N}(\text{CH}_2)_6\text{NH}_2$). Polymerization: Condensation. Reaction: $\text{n HOOC}(\text{CH}_2)_4\text{COOH} + \text{n H}_2\text{N}(\text{CH}_2)_6\text{NH}_2 \rightarrow [\text{-CO}(\text{CH}_2)_4\text{CONH}(\text{CH}_2)_6\text{NH-}]_n + \text{n H}_2\text{O}$. Small molecule lost: Water ($\text{H}_2\text{O}$).

Addition against condensation polymers; monomers of nylon 6,6, polystyrene and Bakelite. Why: six of eight papers (2078 model, 2079 model, 2079, 2081, 2082, model set A).

question: Describe the process of extracting mercury from cinnabar including the temperature range and the nature of the reaction.
answer: Cinnabar is roasted in air at 700–800 K in a shaft or rotary furnace without a reducing agent. The reaction formula is $\text{HgS} + \frac{3}{2}\text{O}_2 \rightarrow \text{Hg} + \text{SO}_2$. Mercury(II) oxide, if formed, decomposes immediately due to its instability.
anchor: Cinnabar is roasted in a current of air at 700–800 K in a shaft or rotary furnace: No reducing agent is needed. Mercury(II) oxide is so unstable that even if it forms first it decomposes at once: Show the data, the formula, the substitution and the unit. The inorganic unit is about extraction and compounds: copper with its blast furnace and matte, zinc with its retort, mercury from cinnabar, iron to steel, and the vitriols.

question: Explain why $Sc^{3+}$, $Ti^{4+}$, $Cu^+$, and $Zn^{2+}$ ions are colorless and classify Zn, Cd, and Hg as transition metals based on their electron configuration.
answer: These ions ($Sc^{3+}$, $Ti^{4+}$, $Cu^+$, $Zn^{2+}$) are colorless due to lack of d-d transitions; their d orbitals are either empty or fully filled. Zn, Cd, Hg are not classified as transition metals because they do not have partially filled d orbitals in their stable ions, despite being in the d-block.
anchor: Colour needs partially filled d orbitals for a d–d transition, so Sc³⁺ (3d⁰), Ti⁴⁺ (3d⁰), Cu⁺ (3d¹⁰) and Zn²⁺ (3d¹⁰) are all colourless. Zn, Cd and Hg have a complete d¹⁰ shell in the atom and in every stable ion they form, so by the IUPAC definition they are not transition elements — they sit in the d block but are not of it. The shape follows from the coordination number and from the hybridisation the metal ion adopts. The same coordination number of four can give either a tetrahedral (sp³) or a square planar (dsp²) complex, depending on the metal ion and the ligand. 6.5 d-orbitals in complex ions (crystal field theory, octahedral complex).

question: Describe the role of silica as a flux in the extraction of copper and the composition of the resulting copper matte.
answer: Silica acts as a flux by reacting with iron to form a fusible slag ($FeO + SiO_2 \rightarrow FeSiO_3$), which is removed. The remaining molten product is copper matte, a mix of $Cu_2S$ and $FeS$, containing approximately 45% copper.
anchor: Silica is the flux; it removes iron as a fusible slag: FeO + SiO₂ → FeSiO₃ (fusible slag, tapped off) The molten product that collects below the slag is copper matte, a mixture of Cu₂S and FeS containing about 45% copper. 4. Zinc: extraction from blende, the vertical retort, white vitriol, lithopone, why zinc is non-typical. Why: 2079 and 2082, each of them a full five-mark question.

question: Explain the formation of azoxy compounds in an alkaline medium and describe the reactivity trend in the substitution of nitroalkanes in DMF using NaNO₂. Include bond lengths in nitro groups in your explanation.
answer: In an alkaline medium, nitroso compounds and hydroxylamine condense to form azoxy compounds, leading to bimolecular products. In DMF, NaNO₂ primarily forms nitroalkanes due to the Kornblum modification, with substitution reactivity following 1° > 2° > 3°, and iodides reacting fastest. The nitro group contains a positively charged nitrogen and a negatively charged oxygen, yet experimental evidence shows both N–O bonds to be identical at 122 pm.
anchor: In the alkaline medium the intermediate nitroso compound and the hydroxylamine condense to give the azoxy compound, which is the reason for the bimolecular products. (In the polar aprotic solvent DMF, NaNO₂ does give mainly the nitroalkane — the Kornblum modification.) Reactivity for the substitution follows 1° > 2° > 3°, and iodides react fastest. In the nitro group the nitrogen is positively charged and one oxygen negatively charged, but the two N–O bonds are found experimentally to be identical (both 122 pm).

question: Describe the stepwise reduction of nitrobenzene under alkaline conditions and electrolytic conditions in strong acid. Include the final products formed in each case.
answer: Under alkaline conditions, nitrobenzene undergoes sequential reduction forming azoxybenzene, azobenzene, and finally hydrazobenzene. In strong acidic electrolytic conditions, nitrobenzene rearranges to form p-aminophenol, which is crucial in the industrial synthesis of paracetamol. The sequence under alkalinity is $\text{NO}_2\text{-C}_6\text{H}_5 \rightarrow \text{N}=\text{O}-\text{N}\text{-C}_6\text{H}_5 \rightarrow \text{N}\equiv\text{N}\text{-C}_6\text{H}_5 \rightarrow \text{N}\text{(H)}=\text{NH}\text{-C}_6\text{H}_5$. Under strong acidic conditions, the product is $\text{p-}\text{NH}_2\text{-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-OH}$.
anchor: Nitro compounds matter for two reasons: they are the standard doorway to amines (and therefore to dyes and drugs), and the nitro group is the textbook example of a strongly deactivating, meta-directing substituent on a benzene ring. Alkaline → two rings couple (azoxy → azo → hydrazo, in order of increasing reduction). Electrolytic in strong acid → the –NHOH rearranges onto the ring, giving p-aminophenol (this is the industrial route to paracetamol). The examiner asks for the reduction of nitrobenzene in different media almost every year (2078 model, 2079 model, 2081, 2082, 2083) and often as a chain question that starts from benzene.

question: Describe the characteristics of organometallic compounds, using ferrocene as an example. Include its synthesis, properties, and why sodium ethoxide is not considered an organometallic compound.
answer: Organometallic compounds feature a direct metal–carbon bond, making carbon electron-rich ($M-C$). Ferrocene, synthesized from $FeCl_2$ and sodium cyclopentadienide, exemplifies this; 1 g $FeCl_2$ yields up to 1.47 g ferrocene. Ferrocene is non-polar, sublimes near 100°C, and dissolves in organic solvents but not water. Sodium ethoxide (Na-O) lacks a metal-carbon bond, thus is not organometallic.
anchor: An organometallic compound contains a direct metal–carbon bond. That single requirement is what makes these compounds so useful: in almost every other organic molecule carbon is the electron-poor end of its bonds, but a metal is less electronegative than carbon, so here the carbon is electron-rich and behaves as a carbanion. The definition is a metal–carbon bond: use it to reject sodium ethoxide (Na–O) in a "which are organometallic" question. Made from iron(II) chloride and sodium cyclopentadienide, 1 g of FeCl2 can give at most 1.47 g of ferrocene. Because the molecule is non-polar and stable, it sublimes near 100 degrees C and dissolves in organic solvents but not in water.Photo credits: (a) Kate7234, CC0.

unit: Nuclear Chemistry and Applications of Radioactivity
question: Describe the decay pattern of Fluorine-18 and explain why it requires production near the point of use.
answer: Fluorine-18 decays via positron emission with a half-life of 109.77 minutes. Its remaining percentage decreases over time: 68.5% after 1 hour, 46.9% after 2 hours, 22.0% after 4 hours, and 10.3% after 6 hours. Due to its short half-life, it must be produced in a nearby cyclotron to ensure sufficient activity at the time of use.
anchor: Radioactivity is the spontaneous disintegration of an unstable nucleus; discovered by Becquerel (1896), it is unaffected by temperature, pressure or chemical combination. (b) Fluorine-18 decays by positron emission with a half-life of 109.77 minutes. The cell shows 68.5 per cent left after 1 hour, 46.9 per cent after 2 hours, 22.0 per cent after 4 hours and only 10.3 per cent after 6 hours, so the patient's exposure is short but the tracer must be made in a cyclotron close to the hospital.

question: Compare the basicity of aliphatic amines, ammonia, and aniline. What is the significance of aniline in the preparation of aromatic compounds?
answer: Aliphatic amines are stronger bases than ammonia, while aniline is weaker. Aniline is crucial for making diazonium salts, used to synthesize various aromatic compounds and dyes.
anchor: Aliphatic amines are stronger bases than ammonia and aniline is weaker, and aniline is a useful starting material for diazonium salts, from which many aromatic compounds and dyes are made.

question: Describe the physical properties of lower ethers and explain Williamson's synthesis for the preparation of ethers.
answer: Lower ethers are colorless, volatile, and very inflammable liquids except methoxymethane and methoxyethane, which are gases at room temperature. They have a sweet smell. Williamson's synthesis involves warming a sodium alkoxide or phenoxide with a haloalkane in dry conditions to form ethers.
anchor: This is cheap and is used industrially, but it works only for simple ethers — a mixture of two alcohols would give all three possible products. Methoxymethane and methoxyethane are gases at room temperature; the rest of the lower ethers are colourless, volatile, very inflammable liquids with a sweet smell. Williamson's synthesis is the general method: a sodium alkoxide or phenoxide (the nucleophile) is warmed with a haloalkane in dry conditions.

question: Given 11.8 g of ethanamide, calculate the theoretical mass of the amine produced when treated with bromine and sodium hydroxide, assuming an 80% yield.
answer: Molar mass of ethanamide (CH3CONH2) = 59 g/mol. Moles of ethanamide = 11.8 g / 59 g/mol = 0.2 mol. Theoretical moles of amine = 0.2 mol. Mass of amine = 0.2 mol * 31 g/mol (CH3CH2NH2) = 6.2 g. Actual mass with 80% yield = 6.2 g * 0.8 = 4.96 g.
anchor: Problem. 11.8 g of ethanamide (acetamide) is treated with bromine and sodium hydroxide. Calculate the mass of amine obtained if the yield is 80 %. A large excess of ammonia is used to push the first step and suppress the rest. If a question asks for a pure primary amine, choose the Hofmann bromamide reaction or reduction of a nitrile or nitro compound instead.

question: Describe the operation of a hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell as used in the Apollo spacecraft and explain why it does not 'run down'.
answer: A hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell is a galvanic cell where hydrogen and oxygen are continuously supplied. It converts chemical energy into electrical energy through reactions at the electrodes without depleting itself, thus it never 'runs down'. $2H_2 + O_2 \rightarrow 2H_2O$ is the overall reaction.
anchor: A fuel cell is a galvanic cell in which the reactants are supplied continuously from outside, so the cell never "runs down". The hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell used on the Apollo spacecraft is the standard example. In electrolysis the polarity of the labels is reversed: there the anode is the positive electrode. "All transition metals and their compounds are coloured" is false, and zinc is not a transition element at all.

question: Explain why the statement 'the heat of the system is 200 J' is incorrect, and describe the principle that governs the conservation of energy in thermodynamic processes.
answer: The statement is incorrect because energy cannot be attributed as 'heat of the system'; instead, it should be stated as 'the system absorbed 200 J of heat'. The principle of conservation of energy asserts that energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transformed between forms. Thermodynamics tracks energy movement and predicts reaction feasibility.
anchor: Saying "the heat of the system is 200 J" is wrong; "the system absorbed 200 J of heat" is right. Energy can neither be created nor destroyed, although it may be converted from one form to another. Burning a cylinder of LPG in a Kathmandu kitchen releases heat; dissolving ammonium nitrate in water makes the beaker go cold. Thermodynamics is the book-keeping that tells us how much energy moves, in which direction, and — most usefully — whether a reaction will happen at all without being pushed.

question: Explain, using resonance structures, why carboxylic acids are more acidic than phenol and ethanol. Additionally, arrange the following compounds in increasing order of acidity and justify your arrangement: CH₃COOH, HCOOH, ClCH₂COOH, (CH₃)₃CCOOH, Cl₃CCOOH.
answer: Carboxylic acids are more acidic than phenol and ethanol due to the delocalization of the negative charge on the conjugate base via resonance, stabilizing it. Resonance structures show the negative charge spreading over two oxygen atoms. The order of increasing acidity is: (CH₃)₃CCOOH < CH₃COOH < HCOOH < ClCH₂COOH < Cl₃CCOOH. This is because the presence of electronegative chlorine increases electron-withdrawing inductive effect, enhancing acidity, while bulkier alkyl groups decrease it.
anchor: They form hydrogen-bonded dimers, so they boil above alcohols of the same molar mass (ethanoic acid 118 °C against propan-1-ol 97 °C). Esters with no α-hydrogen, such as ethyl benzoate, cannot undergo it. Explain, with resonance structures, why a carboxylic acid is more acidic than both phenol and ethanol. Arrange the following in increasing order of acid strength and justify: CH₃COOH, HCOOH, ClCH₂COOH, (CH₃)₃CCOOH, Cl₃CCOOH.

question: Explain why CH₃F does not have the largest dipole moment despite fluorine being the most electronegative atom and describe the role of an alcohol as a base in the elimination reaction to form an alkene.
answer: CH₃F doesn't have the largest dipole moment due to the short C–F bond, minimizing charge separation. Alcohol acts as a base, removing a β-hydrogen ($\beta$-hydrogen) to form an alkene via elimination.
anchor: Fluorine is the most electronegative atom, yet CH₃F does not have the largest dipole moment, because the C–F bond is so short that the charges are not far enough apart. In alcohol it acts as a base, pulling off a β-hydrogen, and you get the alkene (elimination). Losing a mark here is the most avoidable mistake in the whole unit.

question: Explain the principle of thermodynamics used in an instant cold pack and calculate the enthalpy change if 0.5 moles of ammonium nitrate dissolve in water.
answer: The principle used is the total enthalpy change is constant regardless of steps. In a cold pack, squeezing dissolves ammonium nitrate, absorbing 25.7 kJ/mol. For 0.5 moles, $\Delta H = 0.5 \times 25.7 = 12.85$ kJ absorbed, cooling the pack.
anchor: The total enthalpy change of a reaction is the same whether the reaction takes place in one step or in several steps, provided the initial and final states are the same. (a) In an instant cold pack, squeezing the pouch breaks an inner bag and lets ammonium nitrate dissolve in water. (b) The dissolution absorbs 25.7 kJ per mole, so the solution gets colder.

question: Describe the classification of amines based on the number of carbon atoms attached to the nitrogen atom, and explain the significance of the lone pair in amines. Additionally, specify the temperature range required for diazotisation and coupling reactions.
answer: Amines are classified by the number of carbon atoms attached to nitrogen: primary (1), secondary (2), tertiary (3). The lone pair persists in these but is lost in quaternary salts. Diazotisation and coupling require 0–5 °C; omitting this temperature often leads to lost marks.
anchor: Classification of amines by the number of carbon atoms on nitrogen. The lone pair (shown as two dots) survives in all three classes and is lost only in the quaternary salt. Every diazotisation and every coupling must be written at 0–5 °C; omitting the temperature is the commonest lost mark in this unit.

unit: Nuclear Chemistry and Applications of Radioactivity
question: Explain the principles behind nuclear fusion and fission, and describe how alpha, beta, and gamma radiation are shielded.
answer: Nuclear fusion combines two light nuclei into a heavier nucleus, releasing energy through mass-to-energy conversion. Fission splits a heavy nucleus into lighter ones, also converting mass to energy. Alpha particles are halted by paper, beta particles by a few millimeters of aluminum, and gamma rays require thick lead or concrete for attenuation.
anchor: Nuclear fusion is the joining of two light nuclei into a heavier one. Radiation damages cells and can cause cancer, and radioactive waste must be shielded and stored for thousands of years. Fission is the basis of today's nuclear power stations, while fusion promises cleaner energy in the future; both come from the conversion of mass into energy. Alpha particles are stopped by a sheet of paper, beta particles by a few millimetres of aluminium; gamma rays are only attenuated, by thick lead or concrete.

question: A 0.150 g sample of a pure monocarboxylic acid requires 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 M NaOH for complete neutralization. Calculate the molar mass of the acid. (Given: Molarity of NaOH = 0.100 M, Volume of NaOH = 25.0 cm³, Mass of acid = 0.150 g)
answer: 1. Moles of NaOH used = $0.100 \times \frac{25.0}{1000} = 0.0025$ mol. 2. Since the acid is monocarboxylic, moles of acid = 0.0025 mol. 3. Molar mass = $\frac{0.150}{0.0025} = 60.0$ g/mol.
anchor: Problem. 0.150 g of a pure monocarboxylic acid needs exactly 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 M sodium hydroxide for complete neutralisation. Cl⁻ is the conjugate base of a strong acid and so a very weak base — it leaves easily.

question: What are two major uses of nitrobenzene in industrial applications?
answer: Nitrobenzene is used as a starting material for aniline and azo dyes, and it serves as a solvent in shoe and floor polish manufacturing.
anchor: Nitrobenzene is the starting material for aniline and the azo dyes; it is used in shoe and floor polish, as a solvent and in perfumery.

question: Explain why Sc³⁺, Ti⁴⁺, Cu⁺, and Zn²⁺ ions are colorless using the concept of d–d transitions.
answer: Sc³⁺ ($3d^0$), Ti⁴⁺ ($3d^0$), Cu⁺ ($3d^{10}$), and Zn²⁺ ($3d^{10}$) are colorless because they lack partially filled d orbitals necessary for d–d transitions, which are responsible for color in transition metal ions.

Colour needs partially filled d orbitals for a d–d transition, so Sc³⁺ (3d⁰), Ti⁴⁺ (3d⁰), Cu⁺ (3d¹⁰) and Zn²⁺ (3d¹⁰) are all colourless. Zn, Cd and Hg have a complete d¹⁰ shell in the atom and in every stable ion they form, so by the IUPAC definition they are not transition elements — they sit in the d block but are not of it.

question: Explain how diethyl ether should be stored and describe one chemical reaction involving ethers.
answer: Diethyl ether should be stored away from flames due to its high volatility and flammability. Ethers react with HI to cleave, forming alkyl halides and alcohol, essential in the Zeisel method for detecting methoxy groups.

question: Calculate the molar mass of the monocarboxylic acid given that 0.150 g requires 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 M NaOH for complete neutralization.
answer: Moles of NaOH = 0.100 M × 0.025 L = 0.0025 mol. Since 1 mole of acid reacts with 1 mole of NaOH, moles of acid = 0.0025 mol. Molar mass = $\frac{0.150 \text{ g}}{0.0025 \text{ mol}} = 60 \text{ g/mol}$.

question: Describe the preparation of an organomagnesium compound RMgX from R-X and provide the reaction equation when CH₃MgI reacts with water.
answer: RMgX is prepared by reacting R-X with Mg in dry ether. CH₃MgI reacts with H₂O as: CH₃MgI + H₂O → CH₄↑ + Mg(OH)I.
anchor: Preparation: R–X + Mg in dry ether → RMgX; reactivity R–I > R–Br > R–Cl. Any active hydrogen kills the reagent: CH₃MgI + H₂O → CH₄↑ + Mg(OH)I (the basis of Zerewitinoff's method).

question: Explain the mechanism of reactions involving organometallic compounds and describe the role of the carbon atom in these reactions.
answer: In organometallic reactions, a δ- carbon attacks an electron-poor carbon or hydrogen. The carbon, bonded to a less electronegative metal, acts as an electron-rich carbanion. Reaction concludes with hydrolysis of the formed magnesium salt using dilute acid to yield the organic product.
anchor: An organometallic compound contains a direct metal–carbon bond. Every reaction follows the same pattern: the δ- carbon attacks an electron-poor carbon (or hydrogen), giving a magnesium salt, which is then hydrolysed with dilute acid to release the organic product.

question: Explain why Sc³⁺, Ti⁴⁺, Cu⁺, and Zn²⁺ are colorless in aqueous solution and discuss the criteria for an element to be classified as a transition metal according to the IUPAC definition.
answer: Sc³⁺ ($3d^0$), Ti⁴⁺ ($3d^0$), Cu⁺ ($3d^{10}$), and Zn²⁺ ($3d^{10}$) are colorless because they lack partially filled d orbitals necessary for d-d electron transitions which cause color. Elements like Zn, Cd, and Hg, despite being in the d-block, are not considered transition metals under IUPAC criteria because their stable ions do not exhibit partially filled d orbitals. Transition metals typically have incomplete d shells, leading to properties such as variable oxidation states, colored ions due to d-d transitions, and paramagnetism.
anchor: A metal surface has partly filled d orbitals and unsatisfied valencies, so it adsorbs gaseous reactants, holds them close together in the right orientation, and weakens their bonds. Zn, Cd and Hg have a complete d¹⁰ shell in the atom and in every stable ion they form, so by the IUPAC definition they are not transition elements — they sit in the d block but are not of it. Cr and Cu have 4s¹ configurations because half-filled and full d subshells are stable. question: Describe the changes in reactivity when a hydrogen atom in an alkane is replaced by a halogen atom, and list three physical properties of chloroform.
answer: Replacing H in $CH_n$ by a halogen makes it reactive; halogen pulls electrons, making carbon electron-poor. Chloroform is colorless, dense (1.49 g cm⁻³), has b.p. 61 °C, insoluble in water, non-flammable, and dissolves fats, oils, etc.
anchor: Replace one hydrogen of an alkane by a halogen and the molecule stops being inert. The halogen pulls electron density away from the carbon it is attached to, leaving that carbon electron-poor and open to attack by anything carrying a lone pair. Chloroform is a colourless, sweet-smelling, heavy liquid (density 1.49 g cm⁻³, b.p. 61 °C), almost insoluble in water, non-inflammable, and a good solvent for fats, oils, waxes, resins, rubber and iodine.

question: Describe the process of making jaand, chhyang, and raksi from millet and rice using fermentation and distillation techniques. Additionally, identify the type of alcohol A ($C_4H_{10}O$) based on its reactions with Lucas reagent, Victor Meyer's test, and a mixture of $I_2$ and NaOH.
answer: Jaand and chhyang are produced by fermenting millet or rice in the Nepali hills, where yeast converts sugars into ethanol. Raksi is obtained by distilling this fermented wash to concentrate the alcohol content. Alcohol A ($C_4H_{10}O$) is a secondary alcohol as it gives turbidity with Lucas reagent after five minutes, indicating slower reaction rate than primary alcohols. It shows a blue color in Victor Meyer's test, confirming it is a secondary alcohol. The yellow precipitate formed with $I_2$ and NaOH further confirms its secondary nature due to iodoform reaction.

question: Explain the principle of enthalpy change in chemical reactions and illustrate it with examples from everyday life.
answer: The total enthalpy change is constant regardless of the number of steps, if initial and final states remain unchanged. For example, burning LPG releases heat ($\Delta H < 0$), while dissolving ammonium nitrate absorbs heat ($\Delta H > 0$), demonstrating energy flow directions.
anchor: The total enthalpy change of a reaction is the same whether the reaction takes place in one step or in several steps, provided the initial and final states are the same. Burning a cylinder of LPG in a Kathmandu kitchen releases heat; dissolving ammonium nitrate in water makes the beaker go cold. Thermodynamics is the book-keeping that tells us how much energy moves, in which direction, and — most usefully — whether a reaction will happen at all without being pushed.

question: Explain the roles of a positive catalyst, negative catalyst, and a promoter in chemical reactions using examples.
answer: A positive catalyst increases reaction speed, e.g., $\text{Fe}$ in $\text{H}_2\text{O}_2$ decomposition. A negative catalyst (inhibitor) decreases it, e.g., glycerol in $\text{H}_2\text{O}_2$ decomposition. A promoter enhances a catalyst's effect without catalyzing alone, e.g., $\text{Mo}$ with $\text{Fe}$ in ammonia synthesis.
anchor: It is a measure of the intrinsic speed of a reaction, free of the accident of how concentrated the solution happens to be. Two reactions can be compared only through their rate constants, never through their rates. A positive catalyst speeds the reaction up; a negative catalyst (inhibitor) slows it down, as glycerol does for the decomposition of H₂O₂. A promoter (activator) is a substance that has no catalytic power of its own but increases the activity of a catalyst — Mo with Fe in the Haber process.

question: Describe the products formed when 2,2-dimethylpropanal undergoes Cannizzaro's reaction with concentrated alkali and explain why aromatic aldehydes are less reactive than aliphatic ones.
answer: 2,2-Dimethylpropanal undergoes Cannizzaro's reaction as $2(CH_3)_3CCHO + NaOH \rightarrow (CH_3)_3CCH_2OH + (CH_3)_3CCOONa$, yielding 2,2-dimethylpropan-1-ol and sodium 2,2-dimethylpropanoate. Aromatic aldehydes are less reactive due to the electron-donating resonance effect of the aromatic ring, reducing the positive charge on the carbonyl carbon.

Alkyl groups release electrons (+I), so each one reduces the δ+ charge on the carbonyl carbon. In benzaldehyde the ring donates electron density by resonance, which is why an aromatic aldehyde is less reactive than an aliphatic one.

question: Describe the position isomerism in butanoic acid derivatives and mention any four derivatives of carboxylic acids along with their associated named reactions.
answer: Butanoic acid derivatives show position isomerism: 2-chlorobutanoic, 3-chlorobutanoic, and 4-chlorobutanoic acids. Carboxylic acid derivatives include acid halides (Schotten–Baumann reaction), anhydrides, esters (Claisen reaction), and amides (Hofmann bromamide degradation).

question: Explain the operation of a Daniell cell, including the movement of electrons and ions, and define the cell potential.
answer: In a Daniell cell, Zn(s) | Zn²⁺(1 M) || Cu²⁺(1 M) | Cu(s), electrons move from the zinc anode to the copper cathode via an external circuit. Zinc oxidizes at the anode ($Zn(s) \rightarrow Zn^{2+}(aq) + 2e^-$), releasing electrons. At the cathode, copper ions reduce ($Cu^{2+}(aq) + 2e^- \rightarrow Cu(s)$). A salt bridge maintains electrical neutrality by transporting ions. Cell potential, or electromotive force, is the potential difference between electrodes when no current flows, measured as the voltage difference between the anode and cathode.

question: What distinguishes aldehydes from ketones in terms of their structure and how does this affect their chemical behavior?
answer: In aldehydes, the carbonyl carbon has at least one hydrogen ($-CHO$), while in ketones, it has two carbon groups ($R-CO-R'$). This difference affects oxidation reactions, silver mirror tests, and self-condensation.
anchor: In an aldehyde the carbonyl carbon carries at least one hydrogen; in a ketone it carries two carbon groups. That single difference in substitution controls everything in this unit — which reagent oxidises which, which compound gives a silver mirror, and which one condenses with itself.

question: Describe the products formed when primary, secondary, and tertiary alcohols undergo dehydrogenation at 573 K using Cu as a catalyst. Also, explain the result of the iodoform test on alcohol.
answer: Primary alcohols form aldehydes, secondary alcohols form ketones, and tertiary alcohols form alkenes. The iodoform test with I₂ and NaOH yields a yellow CHI₃ precipitate with a medicinal smell for alcohols like CH₃CH(OH)R.
anchor: Dehydrogenation (Cu, 573 K): 1° gives an aldehyde, 2° a ketone and 3° an alkene. Victor Meyer's test to distinguish 1°, 2° and 3° alcohols is the most repeated organic question in the syllabus: it was set in the 2078 model, 2079 model, 2081 and 2083 papers.

question: Explain why the statement 'the heat of the system is 200 J' is incorrect according to thermodynamics principles, and provide an accurate description of the same scenario.
answer: The statement is incorrect because heat refers to energy transfer, not a property of the system. Correctly, 'the system absorbed 200 J of heat'. This aligns with thermodynamics, where energy isn't created or destroyed but can change forms, like in LPG burning or ammonium nitrate dissolving.
anchor: Burning a cylinder of LPG in a Kathmandu kitchen releases heat; dissolving ammonium nitrate in water makes the beaker go cold. Thermodynamics is the book-keeping that tells us how much energy moves, in which direction, and — most usefully — whether a reaction will happen at all without being pushed. Saying "the heat of the system is 200 J" is wrong; "the system absorbed 200 J of heat" is right. Energy can neither be created nor destroyed, although it may be converted from one form to another.

question: Describe the setting process of cement and how it hardens underwater.
answer: Cement sets in 30 minutes to 10 hours and reaches full strength in 28 days due to the gel interlocking into a hard mass. It hardens underwater as it reacts with water rather than drying. This reaction transforms sand, gravel, and water into a solid structure resembling rock.
